title: In Defense of Cannabis Advertising
description: In an article in a recent issue of The Smithsonian Magazine Inside the Quest to Understand the Link Between Cannabis and Schizophrenia, Dr Peter Gr...
content_html_sanitized:
In an article in a recent issue of The Smithsonian Magazine Inside the Quest to Understand the Link Between Cannabis and Schizophrenia, Dr Peter Grinspoon, for whose work I have great respect, and whose father, the late Dr Lester Grinspoon, was a dear friend, wrote that he “believes that advertising for all drugs and alcohol should be banned.

‘Cannabis advertising, along with alcohol and tobacco and pharmaceutical advertising, is really misleading and unhelpful.’


No one should be surprised that I disagree.


First, let me acknowledge an obvious conflict of interest. I am the President of WEED.de, a German web company that carries advertising for cannabis related products and services. 


However, let me add that I have always been politically libertarian, so I did not have to adjust my principles to fit the circumstances. 


Second, I am opposed to advertising and packaging that targets children. It’s unethical, and it’s a waste of money.  There has been a real problem with cannabis gummies being packaged with cartoon characters that appeal to children. Fortunately, there is no lethal dose for cannabis, but there could have been serious injuries, and the industry needs to police itself to prevent such a pointless tragedy. 


(And parents need to use common sense and keep all medications away from children. “Unintentional pediatric poisoning deaths spiked 37 percent in 2021, with 59 children under five years old losing their lives after gaining access to prescribed or illicit drugs.” 

None of those were cannabis related.)


As noted, I am a libertarian and rather pro alcohol, but I will let the alcohol industries make their own arguments. 


However, I also think that cannabis is in a very different situation, in large part because of almost a century of prohibition. 

See Marijuana Prohibition And the Drug War. A Simple Question of Priorities and Lost Opportunities


The most obvious point is the hyperventilation about average THC percentages in the weed that is so much stronger than it used to be back in the sixties when we all thought it was harmless and we just pretended that we were getting high, or something like that.

See  The Perils of Potent Pot Party Line: Blaming Marijuana Legalization for Increase in THC Levels

And

Why People Who Hate Cannabis And/Or Think It Is Dangerous Should Be Opposed To Prohibition


Anything is less dangerous when the consumer is educated, and the percentage of the active ingredient is known. Advertising plays an important part in both. 


And where do we draw the line?


Cannabis is not a single product. On the contrary, there are many different strains and even more possible combinations. And there are a number of different ways to consume it. Think of the possibilities.


Advertising can and should help educate the consumer, and that is especially important for edibles. Ironically, the surge in cannabis related hospitalizations in Canada post legalization has been disproportionately among the elderly. How embarrassing!


Then there is the question of advertising for cannabis consumption venues. These places can play a very important role in integrating cannabis into the broader culture. They provide a place to consume, and reduce the problem of the odor of smoke, which some people find annoying. Go figure.


Finally, whatever the legal age limits, there will always be teens being teenagers. Advertising should not be aimed at children, but they never had problems getting cannabis under prohibition.

See Legalizing Alcohol Made Under Age Drinking Less Dangerous. Legal Cannabis Can Do The Same for Teens Illegally Toking and Vaping. The Dangers of Synthetic Cannabinoids


Finally, brands can be very valuable, which is both a strong incentive for quality control and a guide for educating the consumer. Advertising helps with both.
